ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: camps on the map
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Groups who aren't hostile make camp on the colony's map for a few days: hunters, refugees, prospectors, pilgrims, traders, healers, players, drovers, minstrels, mourners and more.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: A camp is a neighbor for a week. Terms keep the peace, but every term you add makes them warier.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description:
Now and then a group of travelers makes camp somewhere on the colony's map. They walk in, build a fire, beds and whatever their kind needs (a stall, a forge, a prayer spot, a stage), and stay from a few days to about two weeks. A letter asks what the colony makes of them: let them stay, set terms, ask them to move on with a gift or without, or drive them off. Once they're settled, the council window's World page has their camp: trade, terms, gifts, hiring, and asking them to go.
Camps come with world events switched on and the camps setting on. Only one camp at a time, never before day 20, at least 15 days after the last one left, never with enemies on the map, and in any weather but the really extreme (below -30 °C or above 45 °C), poisoned air or a sky on fire (toxic fallout, a volcanic winter, a flashstorm, noxious haze).
They come ready for the weather of their stay, its coldest night and hottest day as the land's seasons and hours bring them. Anyone who wouldn't be comfortable through it puts on a warmer or a cooler layer of their own people's kind (never past their people's craft or the colony's era, and nothing dear): parkas and hats against the cold, dusters and light hats against the heat. For frosty nights they draw their beds in close round the fire, behind a windbreak (their own, or a few lengths of log wall carried with them, where they put up no hut or tent); in hot weather they pick a spot among trees for the shade where there is one. The letter that brings them says what they wear and how they pitch. A camp doesn't come if, dressed as best they can, the stay would still hurt one of them (past the game's own safe range, 10 °C either side of comfortable). It packs up early only when the weather starts to hurt most of them, turns really extreme (below -35 °C or above 50 °C), or the air turns poisonous. When no camp is on the land, the same page says why none has come (danger on the map, the weather, no friendly people, no room, the days since the last) or that the way is open: each such morning at ten there is about one chance in twenty that one arrives.

li.heading: The kinds of camp

table.li: Camp | Who | What they bring
Hunting party | 3 to 5 hunters | Hunt and cut wood; carry each kill back to their butchering spot and dress it there the same day; leave meat now and then
Refugee family | 3 to 6, children too | Their washing laid out by the windbreak; cut wood, leave some for the colony; many will work, some ask to join
Prospectors (medieval and later) | 3 to 5 | A trader among them; they dig at the rock
Pilgrims | 3 to 6 | Pray at their camp, leave herbal medicine
Traders | 3 to 5 | Keep a stall the colony can trade at
Traveling smith (medieval, industrial) | 3 to 4 | Trade; mend a colonist's worn clothes or gear, or walk over and mend one of the colony's damaged buildings for nothing, doors and gates first

Hermit | 1, for up to two weeks | Firewood stacked by the hut's door, left with the hut; at the end of the season, a carved bird left in its crate by the colony's door; leaves meat or herbs, may ask to stay for good
Traveling healers | 2 to 4 | Ease a colonist's everyday ailment for nothing, or leave herbal medicine; a farewell round before they go
A procession of the faithful | 4 to 7, for a few days | Pray at their camp and bless the colony
Traveling players | 3 to 6 | Rehearse, and put on a show the colony is invited to; leave their castle backdrop standing on the old stage
Surveyors (medieval and later) | 2 to 4 | Take sightings in the hills; once per camp, show the colony a seam of ore in its own rock

Salt caravan (tribal and later) | 4 to 7, for 2 to 4 days | 2 or 3 pack beasts tethered by the stash, with bales and fodder beside them and porters carrying bales to the stall; a bulk trader's stall; leave goods from their packs, tell news from the road
Merchants from afar | 3 to 5, for 2 to 5 days | An exotic trader's stall; tell news of far places
Drovers (tribal and later) | 3 to 5, for 2 to 4 days | 3 or 4 head of their herd graze beyond the camp, a dog at a drover's heels, and the drovers' work is out among them; leave milk, wool or a hide
Penitents | 3 to 6, for 2 to 4 days | Pray at their camp, walk round the colony praying for it

Tree-singers (Ideology: only of an ideoligion that holds trees or nature sacred) | 2 to 5, for 2 to 5 days | Sing to the trees, bless the fields, tend an ailment with a leaf and a moss; leave a ring of saplings where their fire was
A traveling healer | 1 or 2, for 3 to 6 days | Ease a colonist's ailment or illness, leave herbal medicine; a farewell round before going
A band of minstrels | 3 to 5, for 2 to 5 days | Play at their fire in the evening: the colony walks over to listen
Mourners passing through | 3 to 6, for a night to three | Keep a vigil by their cart; tell the story of the one they carry; on the way out, plant a sprig of green by the colony's gate

li.after: A good turn comes now and then while things are going well between the camp and the colony. A healer's care, a show, a song and a blessing each leave a small good mood. News from the road is told to a colonist sitting with one of them at the time.

li.heading: A camp that looks lived-in
li.text:
Each kind of camp shows on the map what its letters say. The animals a camp brings are real: a caravan's pack beasts (the kind their own people's caravans use, where the land allows them) tethered by the stash, a drover's herd grazing on wild grass beyond the camp, the drovers' dog at one of their heels. There are never more than 5, only kinds that can stand the weather here, and the camp feeds them from its own stores, so they never go after the colony's crops or food. They walk in with the camp and leave with it. If the colony harms or arrests one of the camp, or their people turn hostile, the animals are walked off the map first, on their own, and never fight anyone. A beast bought from the drovers is one of the herd, the colony's where it stands.
What a camp puts out once it stands (bales and fodder, a woodpile, washing) is theirs, kept out of the colony's hands like the rest of their goods: they pack it up when they go and leave it lying when they flee. Hunters carry each kill back to their butchering spot and dress it there, by day as well as in the evening; caravan porters carry bales between the beasts and the stall.
Some kinds take a last walk when their time is up. The healers' best doctor goes round the colony first: whoever needs wounds seen to (and gets them tended), then the ill, the ailing and the laid up, then those who spent time at their fire, 4 people at most. That round waits for morning, for up to half a day. The mourners and the hermit walk to the colony's door nearest their camp to leave something there. A walk never takes more than 5 hours; then they go whatever happens.
What a camp leaves behind as a gift only comes when it goes in peace at the end of its stay, and its farewell letter says so: the tree-singers' ring of saplings of this land's own trees, the players' castle backdrop (a large wooden sculpture, standing where their stage was), the hermit's carved bird in its crate, and the mourners' sprig, a young rose or daylily, only in its growing season and only where it can grow. These belong to nobody: the colony can claim, keep or clear them. The hermit's woodpile is left with the hut. Each gift also puts the day on the colony calendar ("the hermit's bird", "the tree-singers' ring", "the players' castle", "the mourners' flowers"), kept by walking out to it, until the gift is gone from the map.
The smith's mending is one of their good turns: the smith picks one of the colony's buildings below 90% of its hit points (doors and gates count as half as far away), walks over, works on it for a while and leaves it as good as new, for nothing. If it isn't done within a day, it's given up. Nothing else of the colony's is ever touched.

li.heading: Camps and the world
li.text:
Camps follow what happens in the region. While a famine, a plague, a war, a flood, a drought, a hard winter, a great fire, exiles on the roads or a rebuilding runs, refugees come about three times as often, and their letters say what they fled. Pilgrims, penitents, tree-singers and the procession come more often in a holy year, a great pilgrimage or under a comet, healers in a plague, surveyors along a new road or in a silver rush, traders and caravans in a trading season, a fair or along a new road, drovers on the drove roads and at harvest, minstrels in a season of songs, mourners in a people's mourning, a plague or a war.
With Ideology, pilgrims, penitents and the procession follow one of the world's creeds and name it in their letters, and say so when the colony shares it; penitents of a guilty, a pain-is-virtue or a preaching ideoligion say that too. Tree-singers come only from a people whose ideoligion holds trees, nature or spirits sacred. Without Ideology, their faith goes unnamed.
A camp of a people that remembers one of the colony by name asks for that colonist when it comes, and that colonist goes out to meet them.

li.heading: What the colony can ask of them
li.text: Every kind of camp can be asked for something beyond trade, terms and hiring, from their camp's page on the World page, while they're settled. Who goes is the colonist best at what's asked, else the one who has spent most time at their fire. What people do happens on the map: an evening at their fire is a gathering there, a lesson is the colonist at their teacher's side, bread for the road is carried over to their camp. Each is asked once per camp (the healer's care once a day), some only after a day or so, some only in the evening (4pm to 10pm), and what costs silver costs more for a richer colony.

table.li: Camp | What the colony can ask
Salt caravan | An evening at their fire (recreation); preserved fare for the stores (90 silver); news of the roads ahead (Social practice for the one who asks, a little goodwill)
Merchants from afar | Their charts and almanacs (120 silver: research); supper with the merchants as guests (cooking practice for the colony)
Drovers | A beast from the herd (180 silver): one of the herd grazing by their camp, or one that suits the weather if they have none to spare; a few hours learning herding at their side (Animals)
Penitents | Joining their evening prayer (a small good mood); bread for the road (15 raw food, carried over: goodwill)
Tree-singers | A walk in the woods with them (a small good mood); singing to the fields, with the growers along (Plants practice)
A traveling healer | Seeing a colonist who is ill or ailing (eases it); teaching the colony's best doctor at their side on the rounds (70 silver: Medicine)
A band of minstrels | Playing at a feast (80 silver); a song about the colony, sung at their fire (a good mood: the song travels); a tune taught (Artistic)
Mourners | Sitting vigil with them tonight; standing by the road when they go (goodwill); food for the road (15 raw food)

Hunting party | A colonist sent hunting with them (the colony's best shot and one more go after two head of good game: Shooting practice, and what they bring down is the colony's); their hides (60 silver: 30 leather)
Refugee family | Supper at the colony's table, children and all (goodwill)
Prospectors | A lesson in reading rock at their diggings (Mining); an hour by their cook's pot (Cooking practice)
Pilgrims | Prayers at the side of a colonist who is ill or ailing (an everyday ailment eased, a stranger's blessing); salve for their feet (2 medicine, carried over: goodwill)
Traders | A colonist helping at their stall for the afternoon (Social practice, and a few coins)
Traveling smith | A lesson at the forge (60 silver: Crafting); mending one of the colony's damaged buildings, doors and gates first, for nothing
Hermit | A walk along the hermit's paths, after two days (Plants practice); a hot meal carried out to the hut (once a day)
Traveling healers | Their remedies (60 silver: 5 herbal medicine); a lesson at their table (Medicine)
A procession of the faithful | Their evening hymn at their fire (a stranger's blessing)
Traveling players | A show at the colony's table after supper (80 silver); a small part in their next play (Artistic)
Surveyors | A lesson with the instrument and the chain (Intellectual)

li.after: Each eases the camp's tension and warms them to the colonist who went, and their people remember the kinder ones: a vigil, the road, a supper, a feast, food given, a beast bought, a healer paid to teach.

li.heading: What they ask of the colony
li.text: Now and then a camp asks something of the colony, by letter: on a day when things are calm between them (tension under 55), half a day or more after they arrive, at most one every other day, and only once Rimfolk's last question is 12 hours behind, like any question that can wait. The letter says what they want and who of the colony would go. Grant it, and it plays out like an ask: the camp's own people walk into the colony to do it (to the gate, the water, the fields, the graves, the open ground in the middle of the colony, or one colonist's side), in daylight, for a few hours, and walk back; the week's page shows them coming and there. What they promised comes when they've done it. Say no, and the camp's tension rises (by half as much if the letter just runs out, which counts as a no); a few take it badly enough to cost a little goodwill.

table.li: Camp | What they ask | What comes of it
Hunting party | Cooked food for meat (only when they have 20 meat or more to spare) | 4 of the colony's meals carried to their camp; 35 of their meat set out for the colony
Refugee family | Work for food | They fell trees by their camp, 40 logs for the colony; 20 raw food carried over
Refugee family | Their broken cart mended (after a day) | The colony's best builder carries 20 logs down and mends it at their fire (Construction practice)
Prospectors | A test hole on the colony's side (after a day) | Two of them dig at the edge of the colony for 3 to 4 hours and share what they find: silver most likely, now and then jade or gold
Pilgrims | Prayers at the colony's graves | Up to 6 of them pray at the graves for 1.5 to 2 hours; a stranger's blessing for the colony (recreation, no mood)
Traders | A day's stall at the colony's gate | Their trader and a porter keep the stall there for 6 to 8 hours (trade as usual), and pay 25 silver for the spot
Traveling smith | Steel to work, 40 of it (after a day) | The steel carried down to the smith, who makes a knife of it and brings it over
Hermit | One dose of medicine (after three days) | Carried out to the hut; the hermit warms to the colony
Traveling healers | Practice for their apprentice on a colonist who is ill or ailing | Their two best healers come to the colonist's side: wounds tended, an illness or everyday ailment eased
A procession of the faithful | To carry their icon round the colony's fields | They walk the fields for an hour or two, up to 4 colonists walk with them; a stranger's blessing
Traveling players | An audience for their new play | The colony goes to their stage in the evening (recreation)
Surveyors | A sighting from the middle of the colony | Two of them take sightings for 2 to 3 hours; then, once per camp, they mark a seam of ore in the colony's rock
Salt caravan | Fresh food for salted fare | 25 raw food carried over; 40 pemmican set out for the colony
Drovers | Water for the herd | Two drovers walk the herd to the colony's water (a mod's well first, else shallow water near the colony) for 2 to 3 hours; afterwards milk, wool or a hide

li.after: A request that can't be granted now (nobody ill, no water near the colony, no graves, nothing to survey) isn't asked. While their herd is in the colony's fields, nothing else of theirs is set going.

li.heading: Questions for the council
li.text:
A camp brings questions of its own to the council (with dilemmas on), and every answer costs one side something. One of their people wants to stay when the camp goes on: take them in and the camp resents it, have the colonist who befriended them speak for them, pay the camp for the lost hands, or send them on and that colonist misses them. A purse goes missing from the camp and a colonist is blamed: search the colony, pay for it, stand by your own, or send them down to answer for it. One of theirs is caught in the colony's storeroom. Their beasts get into the colony's ripe fields and stand among the crops until the answer sends them home; the longer they're left, the more they eat. Riders of another people with an old quarrel come by: side with the camp, bring both to the colony's table, ask the camp to move on early, or keep out of it, and each costs goodwill with one people or the other. A child of theirs and a child of the colony become friends (Biotech). Their feast day comes round: the colony's hall, their fire, or not this year. And a camp that took a fee may not be able to pay it: a beast, a day's work, forgiveness, or the terms are the terms (and a proud camp may pack up over it).
What each answer says happens is done on the map: the colonist walks down to the camp, the silver is carried over, the supper is laid, the beasts are walked home. A camp that moves on early leaves no gift behind.

li.heading: Terms, trouble and parting
li.text:
Terms are a fee every five days, a third of their meat, keeping to their side of the camp, or leaving within three days. They may refuse some, proud groups more often, and every term they accept makes things tenser. Tension also grows a little each day they stay; a gift or a kind word eases it. An uneasy camp bends its terms more often, stops doing good turns, and may fall out with a colonist.
Many in a camp will work for the colony for silver, and now and then one asks to join. When their time is up, a camp that's on good terms may ask to stay a little longer. Driving a camp off works, but costs goodwill with their people.
